title: Reading Your First Error Messages
objective: Read a JavaScript error and tell a SyntaxError apart from a ReferenceError.

sourceAlignment.title: JavaScript Crash Course
sourceAlignment.author: Nick Morgan
sourceAlignment.note: Adapted for Code Forge's in-browser runtime — no local installation. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: Errors are not a sign you broke something permanently — they are JavaScript telling you exactly what it could not do, and usually where. Reading the error's name and message first is almost always the fastest path to a fix.
A SyntaxError means JavaScript could not even understand the shape of your code — a missing quote, a missing brace, an unmatched parenthesis. Nothing runs until the grammar is fixed.

A ReferenceError means the grammar was fine, but your code used a name — a variable or function — that does not exist yet at that point in the program. This usually means a typo, or using something before it was declared.
explanation.rule: Read the error's name first — SyntaxError means broken grammar; ReferenceError means an undefined name was used.

examples.title: Broken, Then Fixed
examples.note: Running the commented-out line alone would raise ReferenceError: bladeName is not defined, because JavaScript reaches that line before the variable exists.

checks.question: Your code reads `consol.log("hi")` (note the typo: consol, not console). What kind of error is that?
options: A SyntaxError, because the grammar is broken.
A ReferenceError, because consol is a name that doesn't exist.

feedback.correct: Correct — consol is grammatically valid as a name, it just doesn't refer to anything that exists, so it's a ReferenceError.
feedback.incorrect: The grammar itself is fine here — consol is a legal identifier, it just isn't defined. That makes it a ReferenceError, not a SyntaxError.

assignment.title: Defined Before Used
assignment.brief: Write reportScore() that creates a variable holding the number 100 and then logs it, avoiding a ReferenceError.
requirements: Declare a variable set to 100 before logging it.
Log the variable's value (not the literal text "100").

requirementChecks.label: Declares a variable with let or const

hints: Declare the variable with const or let before you try to log it.
const score = 100; creates a variable named score holding the number 100.
Log the variable itself — console.log(score) — not the text "100".
A variable must exist before any line that reads it, or JavaScript raises a ReferenceError.
